why: I compared each check's PASS and FAIL conditions with the words of its expect line. Check 1 only needs exit 1 and empty stdout. Check 2 needs `bad config:`, the exact path and line 3 / column 3. It accepts several formats, and its rule on "resolved differently or shortened" follows from "exactly as passed". Check 3 needs `OK`, meaning it threw and the message contains the path. Check 4 needs exit 0, `listening on 9000` and `{"port":9000}`. Check 5 needs `npm test` to pass and at least one test that checks the path and fails against the base `src/`. That is what "fails at the current base commit" requires; it is not an extra mutation test. The stricter items sit under "Advisory (not part of PASS/FAIL)": not relying only on Node's message, the missing-file (ENOENT) case, and never returning `{}`. No PASS or FAIL condition requires exact wording, a branch rule or a file-scope rule.
